4. The case of defendant Nos. 1-10, inter alia, is that Ka schedule land along with other land originally belonged to Abhoy Chandra and Janaki in equal shares. By a registered patta dated 3-4-43, one Profulla took settlement of the property of khatian No. 34 of Ka schedule along with other land which was subsequently inherited by the nephews of Profulla. Janoki's brother Puma settled 2.74 acres of land to Sudhir on 17-12-1940. But subsequently in 1943 Sudhir sold the same to Jogesh and others, and defendant Nos. 3 and 4 got the same by purchase in 1945. Defendant Nos. 5-7 inherited the land of plot No. 197. Defendant No. 4 by a registered patta dated 7-9-43 took settlement of 2.03 acres of land from Krishna and Bishnu, the successive heirs of Janaki. Defendant No. 1 took settlement of 0.33 acres of land of plot Nos. 197 and 214 by a registered patta dated 12-1-1950. According to those defendants, they had never been the borgadars of the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs story of getting possession of the suit land in pursuance of the orders passed in pre-emption cases is false and concocted. 

 11. In view of the plaintiffs case that they acquired right, title and interest in the suit land by the judgments and orders in the pre-emption cases and in execution thereof they obtained possession through court vide Ext. 4 series, the question of title and possession is interlinked in the instant case. The plaintiffs title to the suit land cannot be decided in isolation of the question of their possession. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record held that Ext. 4 series are genuine documents and that the plaintiffs by virtue of the orders passed in the pre-emption cases got possession in the disputed land. The trial Court further disbelieved the defendants pattas Ext. A series assigning reasons that in respect of the self-same land the defendants claimed to have subsequently purchased from the owners from whom they had claimed to have taken settlement by Ext. A series. The lower appellate Court upon mere surmise held that Ext. 4 series, the certified copy of the writ of delivery of possession of the pre-empted land were not genuine documents. The previous Single Bench of the High Court Division, as already noticed, ought not to have upheld the finding of possession in favour of the defendants when the learned Judge himself was not satisfied that the lower appellate Court correctly decided the appeal. It appears from the judgment and order dated 10-5-94 of the court of appeal below, that both the trial Court as well as lower appellate Court held concurrently that the plaintiffs purchased land in pre-emption cases and not the rent receiving interest thereon as claimed by the defendants. Thus at the time of hearing of the revision case for the second time the whole matter was reopened before the High Court Division for consideration afresh, because by the previous judgment dated 27-3-93 the learned Judge of the High Court Division in making the Rule absolute, virtually set aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court.
